section.title: The Ministry of Reconciliation
section.sectionRationale: This is the theological summit of the letter. Christ's love compels Paul, for he is convinced that One died for all, and therefore all died; those who live should now live for the One who died and was raised for them. Anyone in Christ is a new creation: the old has passed away and the new has come. All this is from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry and message of reconciliation, so that Paul pleads as an ambassador, be reconciled to God. It closes with the great exchange: God made the sinless Christ to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
section.thesis: Constrained by the love of Christ who died for all so that all died, believers are made new creations and God through Christ reconciles the world to Himself, not counting sins against them; He commits the message of reconciliation to His ambassadors who implore, be reconciled to God, on the ground of the great exchange, that the sinless One was made sin for us so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the love of Christ that compels, for One died for all and all died; the new creation and God's ministry of reconciliation in Christ; and the ambassadors' appeal grounded in the great exchange of 5:21.

units.label: The love of Christ compels us
units.note: One died for all, therefore all died

verses.text: Therefore, since we know what it means to fear the Lord, we try to persuade men. What we are is clear to God, and I hope it is clear to your conscience as well.
We are not commending ourselves to you again. Instead, we are giving you an occasion to be proud of us, so that you can answer those who take pride in appearances rather than in the heart.
If we are out of our mind, it is for God; if we are of sound mind, it is for you.
For Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that One died for all, therefore all died.
And He died for all, that those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them and was raised again.

units.label: New creation and reconciliation
units.note: God reconciling the world to Himself in Christ

verses.text: So from now on we regard no one according to the flesh. Although we once regarded Christ in this way, we do so no longer.
Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!
All this is from God, who {{katallasso|reconciled}} us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation:
that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men’s trespasses against them. And He has committed to us the message of {{katallage|reconciliation}}.

units.label: Ambassadors and the great exchange
units.note: be reconciled to God; He made Him to be sin for us

verses.text: Therefore we are {{presbeuo|ambassadors}} for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God.
God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the {{dikaiosyne|righteousness}} of God.

katallasso.gloss: To reconcile, to change from enmity to friendship, to restore a broken relationship. God is the one who reconciles: He takes the initiative, through Christ, to bring estranged sinners back into peace with Himself. Reconciliation here is not two parties meeting halfway but God removing the barrier of sin by not counting trespasses against us. The offended party Himself provides the way back, which is the wonder of the gospel.

katallage.gloss: Reconciliation, the state of restored relationship and the message that proclaims it. God has given both the ministry and the word of reconciliation, so that the accomplished peace is now announced to the world. It is the good news that God in Christ has dealt with the enmity of sin and opens His arms to sinners. The message calls hearers to receive what God has already achieved: be reconciled to God.

presbeuo.gloss: To be an ambassador, to serve as an official envoy who represents a sovereign and speaks with his authority. Believers are ambassadors for Christ, so that God makes His appeal through them; the messenger carries not his own opinion but the King's own word. The dignity and weight of the calling is immense, for to hear the ambassador is to hear God's own plea, be reconciled to Him.

dikaiosyne.gloss: Righteousness, the status of being right with God, and the very righteousness that belongs to God Himself. In the great exchange the sinless Christ was made sin for us so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God. This is not a righteousness we produce but one credited to us in Christ: our sin reckoned to Him, His righteousness reckoned to us. It is the ground of our acceptance and the heart of the gospel.

basic.context: Paul reaches the heart of his defense and of the gospel itself. He does not preach to commend himself but because the love of Christ leaves him no choice: Christ died for all, so all died, and those who live must now live for Him. Anyone united to Christ is a new creation. Behind it all stands God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and entrusted the message of reconciliation to His servants. So Paul pleads like an ambassador, be reconciled to God, and grounds the plea in the great exchange, that God made the sinless Christ to be sin for us so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
basic.hermeneutics: These verses compress the whole gospel into a few lines, so each phrase repays careful weight. Notice that reconciliation is entirely God's initiative, that new creation language echoes Genesis and the prophets, and that verse 21 states the double imputation at the core of justification. Read the passage as both doctrine, what God has done in Christ, and appeal, the summons to receive it.
basic.originalLanguages: God katallasso, reconciles, sinners to Himself and gives the katallage, the reconciliation, both the accomplished peace and the message about it. Believers are His presbeuo, ambassadors, who speak with the King's authority. And the climax is dikaiosyne, righteousness: the sinless Christ made sin so that in Him we become the righteousness of God.
basic.typology: The new creation fulfils the prophetic promise of new heavens and a new earth and echoes the first creation, now begun in those united to Christ. The sinless one made sin fulfils the sin offering and the scapegoat of the Day of Atonement, on whom the guilt of the people was laid, and answers the pattern of substitution running through the whole sacrificial system.
basic.christ: Christ is everything here. His love compels; His death for all is the turning point of history; His resurrection gives believers a new life to live for Him. He is the one in whom there is new creation, the one through whom God reconciles the world, and above all the one who knew no sin yet was made sin for us. In Him, and only in Him, we become the righteousness of God. The great exchange is the summit of the passage.
basic.god: God is the reconciler, the offended party who Himself provides the way back, not counting our trespasses against us. He is the author of the whole work, from which all this comes, and the one who makes His appeal through His ambassadors. In verse 21 He is the one who made Christ to be sin and who credits His righteousness to us, both just and the justifier of those who are in Christ.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 5 says while we were enemies we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son. Isaiah 53 speaks of the servant on whom the LORD laid the iniquity of us all. Galatians 6 speaks of the new creation. Philippians 3 speaks of a righteousness from God that depends on faith.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible tells how a holy God reconciles a rebellious world to Himself. Here the mystery is unveiled: God in Christ was reconciling the world, laying our sin on the sinless one and giving us His righteousness. Those in Christ are the new creation, the first light of the new world God has promised, and the church is sent as His ambassadors, imploring a lost world to be reconciled to God.

context.literary:
The unit has the shape of a long argument built from small links, each introduced by a little word that carries the logic: therefore in 5:11, for in 5:14, so in 5:16, therefore in 5:17 and again in 5:20, and finally so that in 5:21. Read it as a descent and an ascent. Verses 11 to 13 start with Paul's own conscience before the Lord. Verses 14 to 15 move to the single event that explains him. Verses 16 to 17 draw out what that event does to the way anyone is seen. Verses 18 to 19 climb to God as the one behind it all, and verse 20 turns the whole doctrine into a spoken appeal. Verse 21 then supplies the ground for the appeal.

Two literary habits stand out. The first is the constant pairing of two sides in a single sentence: out of our mind for God, sound mind for you; the old has passed, the new has come; sin and righteousness exchanged in a balanced pair of clauses in 5:21. The second is the shift of pronoun. Paul speaks as we through verse 20, then drops the plural and addresses the Corinthians directly with the imperative, Be reconciled to God. The sentence of 5:18 to 19 is also unusually tangled, with a participle phrase, a that clause, and a second sentence tucked on the end, which shows a mind pressed by the weight of what it is saying. The passage also reaches back to the judgment seat of 5:10 and ahead to the opening of chapter 6, where the appeal is repeated in the plural and sharpened.
context.historical:
Paul writes at a delicate moment. Rival teachers in Corinth have measured an apostle by presence, speech and letters of introduction, and Paul has been accused of being unstable, of weak bearing and of self promotion. The phrase in 5:12 about those who take pride in appearances rather than in the heart is aimed at them. The charge of being out of one's mind in 5:13 may reflect a real accusation, or may point to the ecstatic experiences Paul keeps private; either way he refuses to let it count against the gospel.

The world of reconciliation language was political as well as personal. Ancient writers used the family of words for restoring friendship between estranged people, ending a quarrel between spouses or settling hostilities between cities. Paul takes that vocabulary, which usually describes two parties both bending, and makes it one sided: God alone acts, and the other party is the one in the wrong. The picture of the ambassador also belongs to the period. A Roman emperor's envoy to a province or a foreign court spoke with the authority of the one who sent him, and an insult to the envoy was an insult to the sender. Paul is aware that he is writing to a church that lives in the shadow of imperial power, and he claims a higher sender.

The statement in 5:16 about no longer regarding Christ according to the flesh concerns how Paul once judged Jesus, which was as a failed and cursed pretender, a view he held before the road to Damascus.
context.canonical:
The passage gathers streams from nearly every part of the Old Testament. The language of not counting sins echoes Psalm 32:2, which Paul quotes in Romans 4:8: the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him. The idea of a sinless one who bears sin takes its place beside Isaiah 53:6, where the LORD laid upon His servant the iniquity of us all. New creation draws on Isaiah 43:18 to 19 and Isaiah 65:17, the promise of something wholly new, and Paul uses almost the same phrase in Galatians 6:15, where only a new creation counts.

Within the New Testament, the reconciliation family of words is concentrated in Paul. Romans 5:10 to 11 speaks of enemies reconciled through the death of the Son; Romans 11:15 uses the word of the world; Colossians 1:20 to 22 extends it to all things; and Ephesians 2:14 to 16 applies it to Jew and Gentile made one. This passage is the place where the idea is given its fullest statement as both achievement and mission.

Verse 21 also stands near Romans 3:21 to 26 and Romans 8:3, where God sends His Son as an offering for sin. It has shaped the church's confession on the atonement, from the Fathers' talk of the wonderful exchange through the Reformers' language of imputation to modern discussions of substitution. It also speaks to the end of Scripture, where the One on the throne says, Behold, I make all things new, Revelation 21:5.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the Corinthians to grasp that his manner of ministry, which looks mad or weak to his critics, has one explanation, and that the explanation is not a technique or a temperament but an event. One died, and so everything changed: the way he looks at people, the way he lives, the way he speaks. He is not asking for a favourable verdict on himself. He wants them to be able to answer the people who boast in outward things, and he gives them the material to do it with.

He also intends the passage to work as an appeal and not only as a lecture. The doctrine of 5:18 to 19 is deliberately set in front of the imperative of 5:20. A church that has made peace with Paul but not yet with God has missed the point. The astonishing thing is that the Corinthians, who are already believers, are still being begged to be reconciled. Paul holds together a settled position and a continuing summons, and he wants them to live in both: sure of what God has done, and not casual about it.

Finally, he means to reset their sense of what a minister is. A minister is a messenger whose entire authority is the message, not a patron with a following. By making himself an ambassador he takes himself off the stage and puts the Sender on it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The big statements of this section are descriptions of what God has done once and for all: One died for all, the old has passed away, God was reconciling the world, God made Him to be sin. These are not things believers are told to bring about; they are things they are told to believe and live from. Reading new creation as a command to reinvent oneself turns good news into a burden.

The imperatives are few and plain. Do not live for yourselves but for Him who died and was raised, 5:15. Regard no one according to the flesh, 5:16. And, to the hearers of the appeal, Be reconciled to God, 5:20. The ambassador language is also a role, not a title for a clerical class: the commission is placed on the apostolic circle first, and then extended in the wider New Testament to all who speak the message.

Care is needed with verse 17. Paul says the new has come, but he says elsewhere that the new creation is still groaning, so the passage describes a real beginning, not a finished state. Believers still struggle, and the verse is not a claim that nothing of the old remains in daily life.

debates.question: What does it mean that God made Him to be sin for us?

views.label: Christ bore our sin as our substitute, our guilt imputed to Him
views.case: The historic reading is that God reckoned our sin to the sinless Christ, who bore its penalty in our place, so that His righteousness is reckoned to us; the balanced sentence of verse 21 supports this double imputation.

views.label: Christ was made a sin offering
views.case: The same Greek word can mean sin offering, as the BSB footnote notes, so some render it that God made Christ a sin offering, drawing on the sacrificial system; this still affirms substitution, that the offering bears sin in the sinner's place.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm penal substitution, that the sinless Christ dealt with our sin in our place; the imputation reading foregrounds the exchange that gives us God's own righteousness.

debates.question: How wide is the reconciliation when Paul says God was reconciling the world?

views.label: The gospel is offered to the whole world and accomplished for all who are in Christ
views.case: The world names the scope of the gospel's offer and Christ's sufficient work, while the actual reconciliation is received by faith, be reconciled to God, so the appeal is universal and the enjoyment is by union with Christ.

views.label: World means people of every kind, Jew and Gentile alike
views.case: Others stress that world underlines that reconciliation is not limited to Israel but reaches all nations, so no group is excluded from the message of reconciliation.

debates.bearing: Either way the message goes to all without distinction and is received by being reconciled to God through faith in Christ, so the ambassadors' appeal is pressed on everyone.

study.originalLanguages:
Five phrases repay a slow reading beyond the words the study already names.

The first is synechei in 5:14, translated compels. The verb means to hold together, to press from every side, to confine. It is the verb of being gripped, so that Luke 12:50 uses it of Jesus, how distressed I am until it is accomplished, and Acts 18:5 uses it of Paul gripped by the word. The love of Christ is therefore not a gentle nudge. It confines him so that he has only one road. The genitive, of Christ, can mean Christ's love for us or our love for Him; the context, with its appeal to a death on our behalf, favours His love for us as the pressing force.

The second is the aorist apethanon in the clause all died. The tense speaks of a completed event, not a process, and the construction ties the many to the one: because the One died, the many are reckoned to have died in Him. Compare Romans 6:11 and Galatians 2:20, I have been crucified with Christ. The hyper in on behalf of all, 5:14 and 5:15, is the preposition of representation and substitution together.

The third is the phrase kata sarka in 5:16, according to the flesh. It qualifies the verb of knowing, not the object. Paul is not saying he once knew a fleshly Jesus and now knows a spiritual one; he is saying he used to judge by outward measures and no longer does. That is why it applies to everyone, no one, and not only to Christ.

The fourth is kaine ktisis in 5:17. Kainos means new in quality, fresh, different in kind, rather than merely recent. Ktisis can mean the act of creating or the thing created, so the phrase may be read, there is a new creation, with the weight on God's act. The exclamation Behold, idou, is the signal Isaiah uses before something unprecedented.

The fifth is the little participle me logizomenos in 5:19, not counting. Logizomai is the word of accountancy and law, to reckon to an account, and it is the term Paul uses of faith being credited as righteousness in Romans 4. God has stopped debiting the ledger. The same verb family sits behind the idea in the last verse, where hamartia, sin, is the ordinary word for sin but in the Septuagint is also regularly used for the sin offering, as in Leviticus 4:3. The phrase who knew no sin uses the verb of knowing by experience, so it says Christ never experienced sin as a participant, not merely that he was unaware of it.

typology.type: The Day of Atonement goat, Leviticus 16:21 to 22
typology.fulfillment: On the Day of Atonement the high priest laid both hands on the live goat, confessed over it the iniquities of Israel and sent it away so that it carried them into a solitary place. Paul's sentence that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf is the reality behind that picture: guilt placed on another and borne away. The escalation is that the goat was an animal, chosen by lot, and the transfer was symbolic and had to be repeated each year, while Christ is a willing person who carries the guilt in His own body once for all. The type falls short in that the goat did not die for the sins; only the other goat did. Hebrews supplies the fuller answer by joining both pictures in one Christ.

If the Greek word hamartia in 5:21 is heard as the sin offering, as the Septuagint of Leviticus 4 would allow and the footnote of the BSB mentions, then the verse has Christ standing where the unblemished bull and goat stood in Israel's worship. The offerer laid a hand on the animal, the blood dealt with the defilement, and the worshipper was cleansed. Romans 8:3 speaks the same way when it says God condemned sin in the flesh by sending His Son as an offering for sin. In Christ the escalation is from an animal that could never settle conscience, Hebrews 10:4, to a Son whose offering secures the new creation. The type falls short because it only covered unintentional sin and ceremonial uncleanness; Christ deals with all.

typology.type: New creation, Isaiah 43:18 to 19 and Isaiah 65:17
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah promised something new that God would do, a way in the wilderness, and then new heavens and a new earth where the former things are not remembered. Paul says that promise has begun to be kept in the person who is in Christ: the old has passed away, the new has come. The language also recalls the first creation, where God spoke light into darkness; Paul uses the same picture of conversion in 4:6. The escalation is that the new creation is no longer only a future hope but has a firstfruit in the believer. The type falls short in that the full renewal of heaven and earth is still ahead, Revelation 21:5, so believers live between the beginning and the finish.

typology.type: The ambassador and the messenger of the covenant
typology.fulfillment: Israel's prophets were sent with a word that began, This is what the LORD says, and the messenger carried the full weight of the sender; Isaiah 6:8 shows the commissioning, whom shall I send. Paul stands in that line when he says God is making His appeal through us. The correspondence is that the speaker's own standing is irrelevant; the Sender is everything. The escalation is that the message now is not a warning of coming judgment alone but an announcement that the offended party has already provided the settlement, so the ambassador begs people to accept terms already won. The type falls short in that the prophets were often rejected and killed, while Christ's ambassadors speak from a victory secured.

study.christ:
Christ's love is the first thing the passage names as the driving force. It is not a vague warmth. It is made specific by a death, a death on behalf of all, and Paul reads the cross as an event in which the many were included. That is the pattern of representation that runs through the letter: the one acts, and the many are in him, as Adam acted for all in Romans 5. What the cross does to a person, then, is not only to forgive but to bring a person to an end and begin again, which is why Galatians 2:20 and Romans 6:11 can say the believer has died with Christ.

The second thing is that Christ changes how Christ Himself is known. Paul once judged Jesus by outward measures and found Him a disgrace, a man hung on a tree, Galatians 3:13. The resurrection, to which verse 15 points, reversed that verdict, and once the verdict was reversed all other verdicts by appearance went with it. Seeing no one according to the flesh begins with seeing Christ rightly.

The third is the exchange of 5:21. It must not be softened by turning Christ into a mere example. He is the One who knew no sin, who is therefore able to carry what He does not own, and the passage insists on the double movement: He becomes what we are in our guilt so that we may become what He is in His standing before God. Isaiah 53:6 stands behind it, and Philippians 3:9 shows Paul living on the righteousness from God on the basis of faith rather than on his own record. Romans 3:25 and 26 shows that this is not a legal fiction: God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice to demonstrate His own righteousness, so that He is just and the one who justifies.

The fourth is that Christ is both the substance and the sender of the appeal. The ambassadors speak on behalf of Christ, and Christ's own words, Come to Me, are heard in theirs. Guard against forcing every detail into allegory; the plainest christological claims here are the ones Paul states outright: One died, was raised, is the place we are found, and bore what we owe.
study.god:
The picture of God in these verses has a surprising direction of travel. Everywhere else in the ancient world, an angry deity had to be placated by those who had offended him, and the cost and initiative came from below. Here the initiative and the cost both come from the offended party. God is the subject of every key verb: reconciled, gave, was reconciling, committed, made. That tells us something about His character before it tells us about His plan. He does not wait for a quarrel to cool. He moves toward the wrong, and He does so in a person, in Christ, not at a distance.

Second, the passage holds together two things that people often pull apart. God is the one against whom the offence was committed, and He is the one who pays. The phrase not counting men's trespasses against them does not say sin is trivial or that the debt has been forgotten; it says the debt has been charged to another. Verse 21 shows that the same God who pardons does not do so by pretending. Romans 3:26 states the doctrine plainly: He is just and the one who justifies. A God who simply overlooked evil would be less than holy, and a God who only punished would be less than love. Here the two are not traded off but met in the cross.

Third, God is a God who sends. He speaks through His people as though He were Himself making an appeal. This is a remarkable statement of His humility and nearness: the King pleads, and He uses frail human voices, which Paul has just called jars of clay. Worship, then, takes the shape of wonder and of mission. We thank Him because the offence was ours and the remedy was His. We speak because He is still pleading. And we do both without boasting, since all this is from God, and nothing in it is ours to take credit for.

crossReferences.note: Paul uses the same family of words about enemies and the same event of the Son's death. The extra note here is the reasoning from the greater to the lesser: if reconciliation came while we were enemies, we will be saved by His life now that we are friends. It shows that the peace of 5:18 is not a one off event but the beginning of a standing relationship, so that we also boast in God, Romans 5:11.

In the fourth servant song the guilt of a whole straying flock is placed on one person who is willing to carry it. That gives the picture behind 5:21: sin travels from the guilty to a person who is willing to receive it. Paul changes nothing in the pattern but states it in his own terms, adding the other half of the exchange, namely that righteousness travels back the other way.

David blesses the one whose sin the LORD does not count against him, and Paul reads this in Romans 4:6 to 8 as a description of God crediting righteousness apart from works. When 5:19 says not counting men's trespasses against them, it is picking up that same ledger language and showing it fulfilled on a world scale in Christ.

The laying of hands on the goat and the carrying away of iniquity gave Israel a concrete image for the removal of guilt. Verse 21 stands in that stream: Christ takes what belongs to others and removes it. Hebrews 9 and 10 then show why one offering is enough where the yearly goat was not.

Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything; what counts is a new creation. Paul states the same conviction in a different setting. In Galatians the new creation sets aside the badges of the old identity, and here it sets aside the old way of judging people by outward things, so the two texts reinforce one another.

God says that He is about to do something new and that the former things need not be recalled. This is the prophetic soil of the phrase Behold, the new has come. The Isaiah text adds the image of a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert, showing what the new creation looks like when it arrives in a barren place.

Where 2 Corinthians speaks of reconciling the world, Colossians widens the lens to all things, on earth and in heaven, and then narrows it again to those who were once alienated and are now presented holy. It shows that the same peace made through the blood of the cross is both cosmic and intimate.

Here reconciliation applies to the division between Jew and Gentile, who are made one new man and reconciled to God in one body through the cross. It shows that the ministry of reconciliation has a horizontal edge: a gospel that restores people to God also tears down walls between those who were hostile to one another.

Paul calls himself an ambassador in chains. It sits strangely beside the grand title of 5:20 and shows what the title costs: an ambassador of the crucified King shares His shame, and the ambassador's authority is not found in comfort but in fidelity to the message, which he asks prayer to proclaim fearlessly.

God presented Christ as the atoning sacrifice to demonstrate His righteousness, so that He might be just and the one who justifies. This is the legal and moral grounding for 5:21: the exchange is not arbitrary, and it vindicates God's character in the very act of pardoning.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a world in which God and humanity walk together and ends with a world where the dwelling place of God is with man. Between those two points there is a rupture, and the whole story is the story of how it is healed. These verses stand at the hinge where the healing is declared complete in its decisive act and is sent out as a message.

Looking back, the passage answers the question that Genesis 3 leaves hanging. The man and woman hid from the LORD and were driven out of the garden; the earth itself was cursed because of them. What would it take for God to say, again, I will be their God? Here is the answer: it takes a death that is also an exchange. The sinless One enters the ruin, and those who are in Him are carried out of it. Israel's whole sacrificial system, with its goats and bulls and its Day of Atonement, was a long rehearsal for this single performance, and Isaiah's servant who bears the iniquity of us all was its prophetic portrait.

Looking forward, the passage sets up the mission of the church. If God has already settled the quarrel, then the only thing left is to announce the terms, and the church is the body of messengers doing so. Acts shows the work spreading from Jerusalem to the nations, and Paul's own letters show the cost.

At the end, the new creation of verse 17 reaches its fullness. The One on the throne makes all things new, the old order of tears and death has passed, and the promise of Isaiah 65:17 is kept. Those who were once enemies are at home, and the dwelling place of God is with them. What begins in a single person in Christ ends as a whole renewed world.

quiz.q: What compels Paul in his ministry, according to verse 14?

options.text: The love of Christ, who died for all so that all died.
options.note: Verse 14 names Christ's love as the compelling motive of his ministry.

options.text: His fear of failing the Corinthian church.
options.note: He does fear the Lord, but the compelling force he names is Christ's love.

options.text: His desire to prove himself against his rivals.
options.note: Paul refuses to boast in appearances; Christ's love drives him.

options.text: The reward he expects for his labours.
options.note: His motive is the love of Christ, not personal reward.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by a new creation in verse 17?

options.text: Anyone united to Christ is made new; the old has passed and the new has come.
options.note: Verse 17 declares a real new creation for everyone in Christ.

options.text: A person who has simply turned over a new leaf by effort.
options.note: It is God's creative work in Christ, not mere self improvement.

options.text: Only the apostles are made new in this way.
options.note: It is true of anyone who is in Christ, not apostles alone.

options.text: A promise only for the age to come, with no reality now.
options.note: The new has already come for those in Christ.

options.text: God reconciles us to Himself through Christ, not counting our trespasses against us.
options.note: Verses 18 to 19 make God the reconciler who acts through Christ.

options.text: We reconcile ourselves to God by making amends.
options.note: Reconciliation is God's initiative through Christ, not our amends.

options.text: God and sinners each meet halfway to settle the matter.
options.note: God provides the whole way back; it is not a meeting halfway.

options.text: Reconciliation happens automatically for everyone regardless.
options.note: The message must be received: be reconciled to God.

quiz.q: What is the great exchange described in verse 21?

options.text: The sinless Christ was made sin for us, so that in Him we become the righteousness of God.
options.note: Verse 21 states the double exchange at the heart of the gospel.

options.text: Christ set a perfect example we must now copy to be righteous.
options.note: It is imputation, not merely an example; His righteousness becomes ours.

options.text: God overlooked sin without any cost being paid.
options.note: The cost was borne by Christ, made sin in our place.

options.text: We earn righteousness by our own obedience over time.
options.note: The righteousness is God's, received in Christ, not earned.

questions: Paul says the love of Christ compels him. What would change if the love of Christ, rather than duty or fear, became the driving force of your life?
One died for all, so those who live should live no longer for themselves but for Him. Where are you still living for yourself rather than for Christ?
In Christ you are a new creation; the old has passed away. What old identity or pattern do you need to stop treating as still true of you?
God has made every believer an ambassador with the message of reconciliation. Who in your life needs to hear the appeal, be reconciled to God, from you?
God made the sinless Christ to be sin so that you might become the righteousness of God. How does resting in that exchange free you from trying to establish your own righteousness?

translationNotes.note: The phrase rendered new creation can also be rendered new creature; either way it declares a real, God wrought newness for everyone united to Christ.

God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ describes God as the reconciler who acts through Christ and does not count trespasses; the world marks the universal reach of the message received by faith.

Made Him to be sin can also be rendered a sin offering, as the BSB footnote observes; both readings affirm penal substitution, and the balanced sentence supports the exchange in which our sin is reckoned to Christ and His righteousness, dikaiosyne, to us.
